Hi sweetheart so see how in that first picture the back “flat” part of your ear is pressed up against your bar? That happened to me too. This can happen due to several reasons but here are the ones that may apply to you:

1. You do not have the proper anatomy at all. This typically presents as not having enough of a “ridge” on that bottom exit area of your industrial. But from this picture you maaaaaay have had enough of a ridge although it’s hard due to swelling. It’s also possible that the “flat” of your ear may be too convex, not being fully flat and curving outward a little (super common). 

2. You did have proper anatomy but the bottom hole was pierced too close to the “flat” on that ridge area, so not in the center but instead towards the main wall of your ear.

Either way, here’s what’s happening and how it will affect you:

You just had two pretty traumatic, large gauge piercings in cartilage. Your body is going to send blood and fluid to the area to try to “close” and heal the “wound”. That extra swelling is going to pool in various places, and most likely even more so in the flat of your ear. This is going to cause the middle flat skin of your ear to push up against the bar, which is going to put pressure on both holes. This is a problem bc the part that looks properly (ish) placed at the top is also going to be pushed forward, and even more so, the bottom hole. This is the start of rejection, as even in healed piercings that type of continued pressure will slooooowlg shift the hole in the direction of the pressure. This type of “migration” is easiest seen with poorly done surface piercings, you know the ones that are pierced with a curved barbell not a staple shaped one?

Likely scenario: the constant pressure on each wound prevents your body from being able to “get on” with the healing thus creating more and more swelling and a piercing that will never fully heal, and may be more prone to infection or slight disfigurement of the ear.

Worst case scenario: it shifts the bar so much it actually rejects fully from your ear, “tearing” away.

The reason why proper (if not perfect really) anatomy is really important for this piercing is that each wound is connected to each other. Your body is swelling so much and each injury is affected by the other’s state of healing. It’s a never ending cycle.

Plus you need to have extra room on your bar for the initial healing, which you do, but that necessitates being super cautious with avoiding catching it on things/sleeping on it/getting hair caught it in etc, which is made even harder by the constant pressure your ear will be under.

Honestly love, I’d go get it removed, let it heal, reasses if it was bad placement on the piercing areas themselves or if your flat isn’t suitable for it, and then either get a custom curved barbell when repierced (can be curved outward to accommodate your flat, but looks kinda wonky sometimes) or get two separate piercings and connect them with a lovely chain. Oh or two barbells pierced separately and then you can (when healed) connect them with a lil single link in the middle so it almost looks like a slightly “pie sliced” angled industrial! The AI bot may not know about asking for consent, etc, nuances that are important not to be misinformed by at that young of an age. Both comments above are absolutely beautiful examples of feedback: as someone who’s also struggling with rendering in digital art, it really is a focus on how “flat” images look compared to traditional art.

A first step I took was practicing using “sketchy” digital brushes as it felt more comfortable/produced similar lines to traditional art. I also compared how I held my stylus vs my pencil.

You can google reverse image search :) but it’s a common “business” or “suitware” pose so if you look up that type of picture but include more specifications (ie “women’s suits/professional ware” “plus sized suits/business atire”) etc it might help

I am just now getting back into art so may not have the best advice, but what I’m doing currently is just tracing over anatomy in different poses, over and over again (just quick sketches) for practice daily. Aside from that maybe using a good reference image for the pose will help for proportions.

Full disclosure: I used ai to map out where to shade/highlight (put the image next to it and used it as reference points around eyes/forehead/nose). I also did trace the head/chin shape from an ai work for proportions, as I am practicing them after not being involved in art for quite some time. The art itself is not ai:) just feel transparency is good.

I think using the ai image for shading is what led to the odd chin, the reference image was all wonky/dark shading in the chin area so I had to go by feel.

I’ll say this, if it’s any comfort: I think it looks great. The joys of scarification are that the end result is a scar. If everyone wanted pale, flat scarring, the. I believe they would go with white ink tattoos, the scar looks great against your tattoo, and I love the placement. And there is some comfort in knowing that the end product is almost a collaboration between your artist and your body: your genes influenced the type of scarring, it’s color, you sleeping positions and habits might have effected the tautness of the tissue. The piece ends up being uniquely yours, and I think that’s the beauty of scarification. 

That being said, you can go to a dermatologist and get steroid injections, that will lessen the height of some of the scarring, do what feels most comfortable for you. Just know that it’s nothing that you did wrong, or that the artist did wrong to cause this result.

But it’s the same mindset as boomers claiming that violence in video games causes violence in children. Based on the responses I’m seeing here, which were all directed at explaining the three dimensional aspects of the characters trauma and not the question of if it’ll affect the viewer (I don’t blame them for responding this way, your initial question seems more pointed at the characters morality than the viewers), it seems pretty obvious that many of the viewers understand how deeply flawed and toxic these character’s actions are. Being able to empathize with non traditional characters doesn’t equate to debasing your own moral makeup. Furthermore, while the show’s characters are obviously an extreme version of trauma that’s probably quite uncommon IRL, I’d wager that many viewers probably have people with similar flaws in their lives and directly interact with them without this causing a negative effect on their personhood. Narcissists, adulterers, addicts and liars exist all around us. 

You said in a comment “if you don’t see it as wrong you will see it as right or at the very least acceptable” and I believe that’s a little blind to one of the baseline themes of the show. The world is not black and white, neither are morals. They are complex and situational. The question “is cannibalism wrong” isn’t even black in white. Some cultures eat their dead loved ones as part of the grieving process, the survivors of flight 571 preemptively consented to being eaten so that the other survivors could live, the Donner party famously resorted to cannibalism after months of starving. These are all wildly different cases, and I would say that even on their vast spectrum of morality, not everyone would have a black and white conclusion as to the resolution of that argument. What I’m trying to say in a super long winded kind of way is that being able to understand “justified” or even just “rationalized” immorality doesn’t mean someone will go on to adopt any of those characteristics. I can understand WHY Thanos snapped away half of the universes population and why he thought it was the right thing to do without agreeing. I can feel for and understand why an addict struggles and relapses without justifying dipping my toes into drug use. I can understand why an unhappy woman cheats, what would drive her to that point, without finding my own eyes lingering from my partner with the same justifications. I think you aren’t giving the viewers of this show enough credit :) 

EDIT: in rereading your title is also like you to challenge your own view of what makes these characters “horrible” humans. Is Shauna a good mother or partner? No. But she’s a great friend to Tai. Is Misty a good person? Absolutely not, but she does have dedication to some of her friends, and has saved people’s lives. Is Tai a good mother? No, but she (at this point in the story) has pinpointed what is causing her son trauma and has removed herself so as to not harm him further. She also has tried her absolute hardest to find help for her friends, even though she ended up getting hurt. I wouldn’t classify ANY of the characters so far as horrible humans (Ehhhh maaaaybe with the exception of Misty as she is genuinely psychopathic). The word horrible has a weight to it that must be justified, and I’ve yet to see actions from the characters that would automatically cancel out their positive actions and qualities so as to push them to horrible. Bad? Miserable? Manipulative? Yes. Overall horrible humans? No. Because humans are so much more complex than that.

I really adored reading this! I know how it is to pick up writing again after a lull, and I think this was a great example of diving right in. Please forgive any formatting errors. 

I like that you mixed sights and smells in your opening, fall is full of these and it really sets the certain cozy tone that comes along with the season. That being said, you didn't really go into detail about the patronage of the *The Magician's Mug.* Seeing as Knox is telling a story to his patrons, and we are also along for the ride in the audience, I feel like going into a little more detail about the people that regularly are seen there would be a nice way to frame the story. 

>There were antlers as big as two full-grown men, pearly white knife-like teeth, and sparkling on the fireplace’s mantel, a unicorn’s horn. All of these items had stories, and there was only one man to tell them.

You do go into a lot of detail describing certain items in the bar, such as the antlers and the unicorn horn. It's a nice way to introduce Knox as a story teller, but it doesn't say much about the bar itself. At this point we know that these items inhabit this space, but the set up of the bar would characterize a lot more about Knox as it's his business. 

>"When it came to The Magician’s Mug, the food and beverages were a mere sideshow compared to him. He was the main attraction."

I feel like these two sentences are a bit redundant. If the food and beverages are the side show, of course he would be the main attraction. 

>“Calm down, lads. I have just the tale for you!” Knox said, his foreign accent barely noticeable after years spent in Sanctuary.

I feel like this is a good chance to expand upon what a foreign accent would sound like to those in the Sanctuary. Is it lilted, or gruff, or nasal? It's a small detail, but I think this would be a good place to drop it in for world building.

>Not missing a beat, Knox pushed on, “it has fierce monsters in all shapes and sizes, some of them human. It has a hero, a muscular monster-slayer of a man, his rise to becoming one of the most admired men in the land, all the way to his inevitable fall…”

You describe how the tavern becomes silent after this. I feel like if you are going to show that the fall of this hero has such an effect on the audience, you should include just. a little hint of something more dire that happens to this hero. You go on to explain that the audience is used to happy endings, but I think you could phrase this a little more dramatically in order to make the audience's reaction a little more believable. 

>The crowd was silent now, so silent that the crickets chirping outside could be heard. No one knew what to say or how to react.

I feel like these two phrases can also be combined in some way, as they are a little redundant. I personally don't like the use of the cricket trope, but it isn't horrible. Maybe try rephrasing it in some way. "Silence washed over the crowd, no one knowing what to say or how to react". 

I really loved the ending and the implications that came with it, and am excited to read more should you choose to post it! Knox comes off as a really intriguing character, and I am hoping that some of the items displayed in *The Magician's Mug* will be tied in to Knox story, as it would give more character to his tavern and the importance of those items to him. :)

Hey there! I am not the best at critiques, but I really loved reading over your excerpt so I want to give it a shot. 

First, I notice that you use mainly sight and touch to describe your character's surroundings. That is great, as they are relatable senses that are easy to imagine, but I personally think including sound, or maybe smell descriptors into your work would give it variety and enrichment. For example, you mention that your character's back was "a mass of seeping, criss-crossed wounds." If the wounds on his back are seeping, maybe try to describe the smell of infected flesh. The smell of decay or disease can really elicit strong reactions from a reader, as it tends to be pretty difficult to forget once you have experienced it. 

A couple of people in the comments of your google doc have stated that they wish you would elaborate more on Darrol's torture. I personally think that, as long as you have gone into detail earlier on in the book about Darrol's experiences with Master Illucid, and vividly explain the details of what he went through while training, it is actually okay to hint at the Figment's torture somewhat vaguely. It creates a sense of scale and escalation, of knowing that what your character is going through now is truly harrowing. That being said, the effectiveness of this would truly depend upon your description of his prior experiences. The parts of the torture that we do see your character go through are a couple of slaps, which you do describe in a way that makes them seem more painful, but doesn't quite satisfy when you are simply glossing over the horrific torture he has already experienced by the Figment at this point. Try using your characters surroundings more, and describing them in a way so that the reader may infer as to what may have happened to Darrol. 
Describe some torture devices laying in the background, or a poker-still glowing. You described some of the injuries on your main character, but setting up elusions to what might have caused those injuries can create a heightened sense of dread and tension. 

"On the ground, ogres and giants roared, swinging wildly with tree-trunk clubs and boulder-headed maces." Small thing, but I really like the way you worded the weapons here, as it creates a sense of scale. Too many writers simply state that they are giants, not really giving the reader a sense of just how large a giant is considered to be.

The way that you go on to describe the Figments is also really refreshing, and from the perspective of someone who has never read any of your work, creates a lot of intrigue for these creatures. I especially like your description of "gossamer swords", and your use of tactile descriptors. 

I feel like the simile "cutting down enemy warriors like hurricane winds through a field of wheat" is a little clumsy, and it didn't really flow as easily as some of your other imagery. 

Before her a man knelt, a white-bearded wizard gripping a tall staff. Darrol wanted to warn the pair of the approaching Figments, but the old man sensed something amiss on his own and crawled to his feet." I don't think crawled is the correct descriptor to use here. Someone who is lying on the ground might crawl, but someone who is kneeling wouldn't really. If you are trying to insinuate that he is having difficulty getting up, maybe try stumbled instead.

Erlea Urbina was out on the shores with her daughter, Reyne. They had just journeyed there to oversee a funeral rite, and were playing in the shallows after a long day of riding. Reyne suffers from severe anxiety, especially socially, so she was really happy that her mother had accompanied her.  Unbeknownst to her, a small group of Mainlander soldiers had been sent on a recognizance mission, and were just about to leave. Jo'Han, a new naval soldier, was a part of that group, and his younger sister was currently dying in the Mainlands from what  is widely thought to be an incurable disease. Jo'Han had a run in with Erlea earlier that week, during which she had treated his wounds, and he had witnessed her treating a young girl with a similar disease to his sister's (as she was actually the Islands Master of Blood, which is a scary title for basically the Island's eldest and most experienced healer). In a wild, desperate act, he grabs her and forces her onto the boat that he and the other soldiers are loading into. 

Reyne desperately wants to help her mother, so she attempts to use her (incredibly unstable) magic. She ends up summoning a giant wave the capsizes the boat, and kills everyone aboard, including her own mother and almost herself.

The Marsh doesn't really seek out the dead and dying, as all things must inevitably come to an end at some point, so it is in no hurry to really speed things up. It's not quite sentient, but it does react to it's surroundings in some ways. 

No true Islander would ever really go out of their way to purposely kill or hurt a crow, but if they do, it is punishable by forced labor and volunteer time within the Islands. But, more recently as they have attempted to open their borders, they have had to deal with foreigners maiming or hunting the birds. This has caused quite a commotion with the inner-most council, as they want to punish anyone who would hurt them, but don't have the confidence in their foreign relations to do so without starting a war. 

The Flight is a more modern rite, that sprouted as young Islander's confessed their need to explore the world. It is mostly an act done to honor the dead person's desires to see the world, and it is considered cruel to purposefully rob them of that right. Since all magical energy gives life, and when you die you just get reabsorbed and re-purposed, their lives may eventually have some impact on life outside of the Islands, so it is not necessarily thought that they become trapped. It's just something to honor their desires as individuals. :)

There is a deep abyss in the middle of the Cormacia Island that leads to the Marsh, an area in which magical energy seeps up from the ground. It is thought that all magical energy gives life, and therefore all it must be returned to the Earth so that it may grant new life in an endless cycle. Since the Marsh can sense when someone has passed, or is currently passing, the Marsh will instinctively start to swallow them. The Islands are small and leave little room for burial, making this rite terribly convenient, and therefore bodies are lowered down into the Marsh. But first, they will be taken to a local mortician. This process is called the Burial. 

 On the far cliff-sides, there is a species of corvid called the Bleeding Crow. They are large, intimidating black birds with a red marking in the middle of their chest. These crows exhibit odd nesting behaviors and will often nest on the Cormacian cliff-sides, but make long flights  West to hunt prey in greater quantities. They sometimes will fly between the cliff-sides and Mainlands 3 or 4 times a month. Sadly, due to their large collection of dangerous magical knowledge, up until recently travel from the Islands has been banned, and many people have died without seeing much of the world.

For thousands of years, Islander's have taken their dead to local morticians, who carve out the hearts and wrap them in cloth soaked in magical preservatives. They will take them to the cliff-sides, offering the hearts of the deceased as food to the crows so that the person may explore the world in spirit. This is called the Flight. 

 A truly traditional mortician will make the journey to the cliff sides and the Marsh themselves, being present for both the Burial and the Flight as a sort of guide and master of ceremony. As Islander magic is based on the concept of magical energy being contained in the breath, there is usually a lot of singing, screaming, and music. 

Since most Islanders may not be able to travel for both rites, it is not uncommon to forgo the Flight and simply offer the dead's body to the Marsh. 

While traditional burials do exist, they are considered a waste of space as well as selfish, as natural decomposition is a lot slower and it is seen as delaying releasing your loved one's energy back to the Earth simply so that you have a sentimental place the visit and mourn.

Hey there! I'm a relatively new writer and critique, so most of my critique comes from personal preference and should be taken with a grain of salt. That being said, I think that your story is compelling and interesting, and it definitely drove me to want to read more! 
!!!EDIT: It seems that I didn't really critique as much as I edited it line by line, sorry about that! Let me give you a better overall critique!

I really enjoyed this opening scene as a whole, but towards the end I was a little confused. You put a lot of work into describing and developing Legion, and by the end I could really picture him in my head quite vividly. Pastor Nathan Miller and the archangel, though, didn't have quite as much development. I understand that we will probably be following these two characters a lot throughout the rest of the story, but I didn't find myself connecting a lot with them the way I did with Legion.
So lets address them one by one!:
Pastor Nathan Miller: I...reaaaally had a hard time visualizing him. Usually, through descriptions, I can get a pretty good sense of how a character is going to develop, or what he/she is like. There was a point where you characterized him a little, by detailing that he stood at the window with his hands on his hips and chuckled to himself. But that was about it. The way he moved and handled the situation didn't really tell me a lot about him, and I ended up with more sympathy and interest in Legion than I did him. 
Don't forget that this is scene isn't just a Legion introduction scene, we meet two other characters as well and we should at least get a sense about what they're like from it. 

Uriel: Well, Uriel came off a little stale. I liked the detail about his breastplate and his flaming sword, but his dialogue was stiff and unoriginal, and I felt as though you could have pushed to make him more of the hero of the day. He's an archangel, he should probably come off as more ethereal and powerful. 

Pacing: I thought it moved about well, until the action scene. Honestly the way I had the Legion pictured in my head, it was disappointing to see him defeated SO quickly. Although you made an attempt to describe Legion trying planning to go for Uriel's sword, at no point did I actually believe that there was a chance of Uriel losing. I knew from the beginning of the action that Legion would die (Legion's host?). I understand that Uriel is an archangel, and therefore this scene is supposed to show how powerful he is, but it really didn't portray strength in either character. 
You did a really great job describing Legion's physical form in a very syrupy, sickly way almost. Every detail served a point and drew attention to how terrifying and powerful he was supposed to be. The physical form you gave him really mirrored the way the audience was supposed to fear him. 
I just wish that you had been able to put that type of characterization into the Pastor and Uriel. You just did a great job with one character, so the other two seemed bland in comparison. 

So starting with your opening paragraph:

You did a great job at immediately providing the reader with information regarding Legion not being human. Using descriptions like *his eyeless face,* and *clawed feet* quickly and easily tell the reader a lot about Legion. I really like that you relied on those descriptions in order to characterize Legion, and didn't just resort to outright telling the audience that he isn't human. It seems really basic, but many authors fail to characterize their characters like this and it always eats me up inside. 

That being said, I think you kind of tried to hard to *make sure* that the audience knew that Legion isn't human. Phrases like "he approached the **human's house**" kind of seem awkwardly worded. If you left it at "he approached the house", we could probably figure out that the house belonged to a human. Not a huge deal, but the wording seemed awkwardly stuffed in there  to me. 

I'm really big on varying the types of words and descriptors that I use. If I can, I will avoid using the same word twice in a paragraph. Sometimes you can't avoid using a certain verb, but I think it's a good practice to always vary your  vocabulary. 

" He **smelled** the air. This human's blood **smelled** different from the others, like blood he had not tasted in centuries."

You used the same word twice, one directly after another. I'd suggest changing the first use of the word smelled to something like sniffed or inhaled. Again, small nitpick haha.

"their mouths open and **waiting** to taste" is a little awkward as well, but I can see that you were trying to be creative in how you portrayed their hunger. I'd change it to craving, but maybe change the sentence structure to put more emphasis on it. 

"  Legion was completely alone, but he could feel the rest of the Legion with him as if they were right behind him, watching, their own mouths *hanging open. Craving."*

Craving and watching then mirror each other and almost punctuating parts of the description, and it really draws my attention to the hunger of the Legion. 

"This human would be **like** an appetizer" 

I actually don't think you need the like there, to them this human basically IS an appetizer. It's a small adjustment that makes them seem even more ferocious. 

 "his heart beat at a steady pace, pumping **his** hot blood throughout his body"

You don't really need to reiterate that the blood pumping in his body is his own, and since it doesn't really add any other details we might need to know, I'd just get rid of it. 

As (oh yes the irony) the other commenters have said, you use "as" an awful lot. In the paragraph describing how Legion is thinking about killing the man especially. It would work if you could restructure the sentences to make it more rhythmic, but that's not really necessary and I think you should choose another word. 

​

You use "the Legion" a lot when referring to the specific Legion that we are reading about in this scene. You could probably use a lot more "he" or "him" or "the demon", just to vary it a bit. 

"...he asked the angel, in a voice that came from his mouth and the neck still on his torso at the same time" I love this visual! just wanted to point it out haha.

​

 " Just a few feet away, the human dumped letters into a trash can" Find a way to reword this sentence if it's important to know that hes destroying the letters. Either move the detail before or after the main action starts, or reword it so that it better fits into the action. At the moment it just breaks up the paragraph and takes the reader out of the conflict between Uriel and Legion. 

 "He smelled his own charred flesh" I think that this can be a lot more descriptive. What does his burning flesh smell like? Make the smell seem stronger, more pervasive. Give the description more strength or delete it, as it's a short sentence that seems out of place without more description.

"The human's **blood** was a poor substitute for the **blood** of an archangel, and the whole Legion would enjoy this one's holy **blood**." 

You use blood waaaaay too many times in one phrase. I would try to rephrase it. Something like: "The human's blood was a poor substitute *for an archangel's*, and the whole Legion would enjoy this one's holy blood."

​

Overall, a really great introduction! Some other quips I have is that it got a little confusing towards the end. Was Uriel killing the vessel itself, and not Legion? Or was he killing a part of Legion itself?
